I've gathered substantial material from Enduring Word, Bible.org, Ellicott, Gill, Spurgeon, and Desiring God. Due to search limits, I wasn't able to reach Catholic/Orthodox or modern-scholarship sites directly. Here are the verse-by-verse notes:

---

## Isaiah 40 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### vv. 1–2: Comfort Announced

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"Comfort, comfort My people"** — The doubled imperative marks a dramatic tonal shift. Isaiah 1–39 is predominantly judgment; chapter 40 opens the "Book of Consolation" (chs. 40–66). God is not finished speaking; He now speaks comfort. (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-40/

- **"My people"** — Ellicott notes this is an echo of Hosea 2:1: "Lo-Ammi" ("not my people") has become "Ammi" ("my people"). The covenant relationship is restored. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"Speak tenderly to Jerusalem"** — Literally "speak to the heart," like a young man wooing his beloved (Genesis 34:3). The comfort is intimate and personal. (Enduring Word, Bible.org) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-40/ ; https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-40

- **"Her warfare is ended"** — The Hebrew noun can mean "warfare," "hard service," or "compulsory labour." Ellicott says the exile was "one long campaign" of suffering. The word also echoes Job 7:1 and 14:14, where life itself is a term of hard service. (Ellicott, Bible.org) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm ; https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-40

- **"Her iniquity is pardoned"** — Literally "paid off" or "accepted." Ellicott explains: it does not mean exemption from punishment, but that the punishment has been accepted as sufficient and has done its work. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"Double for all her sins"** — Motyer (cited by Guzik) notes that "double" means "to fold over, fold in half" (Exodus 26:9); each half corresponds exactly to the other — exact correspondence between sin and payment. Guzik adds that under the New Covenant, it is Christ who received the "double" from the LORD's hand, not the believer. (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-40/

- **Gill** reads this Messianically: the "warfare" is the servitude of the law ended by Christ; the "iniquity pardoned" is through Christ's sacrifice; the "double" is the complete satisfaction made by Christ. (Gill) https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/40.htm

**Denominational Notes:**

- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** In his sermon "Comfort Proclaimed," Spurgeon emphasizes that only those who can say "My God" through faith in Christ can claim this comfort. It is not a universal comfort but a covenant comfort for God's people. (Spurgeon) https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/comfort-proclaimed

- **Piper (Reformed Baptist):** Sees the glory-revelation of v.5 as ultimately fulfilled at Christ's second coming, when every person will see it together — for some it will be judgment, for others unspeakable joy. (Desiring God) https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/three-meditations-on-the-messiah

---

### vv. 3–5: The Voice in the Wilderness

**Traditional Reading:**

- All four Gospels apply v.3 directly to **John the Baptist** (Matt 3:3; Mark 1:3; Luke 3:3–6; John 1:23). The herald is deliberately unnamed — John was content to be "a voice or nothing." (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"In the wilderness prepare the way"** — Ellicott notes that Hebrew parallelism favours the punctuation: "A voice of one crying, 'In the wilderness, prepare ye the way…'" The image is drawn from Eastern kings who had roads built through trackless deserts ahead of their royal processions. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"Every valley… every mountain"** (v.4) — Ellicott calls this "a parable hardly veiled": the meek exalted, the proud brought low, wrong ways righted, rough natures smoothed. This is the true preparation for the Lord's coming. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"The glory of the LORD shall be revealed"** (v.5) — Ellicott asks whether Isaiah envisioned the Shekinah glory-cloud of the Temple or had risen to "the glory of character and will, of holiness and love" (anticipating John 1:14). **All flesh** marks a growing universalism in Isaiah's thought — the revelation is not for Israel only. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **Gill** says John prepared the way by preaching repentance, administering baptism, and pointing to the Messiah. (Gill) https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/40.htm

- **Bible.org** notes that Ezekiel saw God's glory leave the Temple and move east with the exiles (Ezek 10–11); here God is returning. The highway language is a metaphor for the "new Exodus." (Bible.org) https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-40

**Denominational Notes:**

- **Piper (Reformed Baptist):** The "glory of the LORD" in v.5 is ultimately the glory of Jesus Christ. Psalm 19:1 says the heavens already declare God's glory, but Isaiah foresees a unique, climactic revelation that "all flesh shall see together" — no longer just Moses, Ezekiel, or Paul having solitary visions. (Desiring God) https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/three-meditations-on-the-messiah

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik):** Guzik stresses that "any great work of God begins with great preparation." The road-building imagery applies to heart preparation: it is expensive, deals with varied terrain, and requires an expert engineer — the Holy Spirit. (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-40/

---

### vv. 6–8: The Frailty of Flesh, the Permanence of God's Word

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"All flesh is grass"** — Ellicott notes this is the "ever-recurring contrast between the transitoriness of man and the eternity of God." The similitude is found in Job 14:2 and Psalm 103:15–16. Ellicott also observes the "naturalness of the thought in one who, like Isaiah, was looking back in extreme old age upon the generations he had survived." (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"The breath of the LORD blows upon it"** (v.7) — Ellicott insists this should be "breath" or "wind" of Jehovah, not "Spirit," since the agency is destructive: a mighty storm-blast tearing up grass. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"The word of our God stands forever"** (v.8) — God's promises are sure even amidst judgment. Bible.org connects this to Psalm 103:17–18, Isaiah 55:8–11, and Matthew 24:35. (Bible.org) https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-40

- **Gill** sees this as the message every Gospel minister must preach: human frailty, the insufficiency of self-righteousness, and the need of divine power in regeneration. Peter quotes this in 1 Peter 1:23–25 to show that the "incorruptible seed" of the Word produces new birth. (Gill) https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/40.htm

**Denominational Notes:**

- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** In "The Withering Work of the Spirit," Spurgeon argues the primary meaning is not merely human mortality but something deeper: the Spirit blows on the flesh (the carnal mind, human pride) to wither all human glory, making room for divine glory. This is the Spirit's preparatory work so that "the glory of the Lord should be revealed and human pride be forever confounded." (Spurgeon) https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-withering-work-of-the-spirit

- In his sermon "Man Transient: God's Word Eternal," Spurgeon adds: "everything especially in which man glories … shall also pass away." The Bible's survival through centuries of persecution proves its divine origin — "the anvil that has worn out many hammers." (Spurgeon) https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/man-transient-gods-word-eternal

---

### vv. 9–11: Behold Your God — King and Shepherd

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"O Zion, herald of good news"** (v.9) — Ellicott notes this is the first occurrence of the Hebrew verb *basar* ("bring good tidings"), which through the LXX (*euangelizesthai*) gave us the word "evangelise" / "Gospel." Zion herself becomes the bearer of good tidings to the other cities of Judah. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"Behold your God!"** — Ellicott says this has only an "ideal fulfilment" in the return from exile, but the prophet contemplates God's renewed presence in the sanctuary. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"The Lord GOD comes with might"** (v.10) — "Adonai YHWH," a combination characteristic of Isaiah. His arm rules; His reward and recompense accompany Him. Bible.org notes this is quoted in Revelation 22:12. (Ellicott, Bible.org) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm ; https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-40

- **"He tends His flock like a shepherd"** (v.11) — The mighty warrior of v.10 is also the tender Shepherd. Ellicott calls Psalm 23 the great OT embodiment of this image and John 10 its NT counterpart. The special care for lambs and nursing ewes echoes Jacob's plea in Genesis 33:13. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **Guzik** notes: "He gathers the lambs in His arms and carries them close to His heart. He doesn't cast the weak lambs over His shoulder … He lovingly cradles them in His bosom, close to His heart." He quotes Spurgeon: "To carry is kindness, but to carry in the bosom is loving-kindness." (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-40/

- **Bible.org** connects this to Ezekiel 34, where YHWH first judges false shepherds, then Himself becomes the Shepherd, then appoints His Messiah (Ezek 34:23–24). Jesus is the "Good Shepherd" (John 10) and the "wounded shepherd" of Zechariah 11–12 and Isaiah 53. (Bible.org) https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-40

---

### vv. 12–17: The Incomparable Creator

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"Who has measured the waters…?"** (v.12) — A series of questions expecting the answer "No one." Ellicott notes the whole passage parallels Job 38–41. The Creator is the "great Work-master of the universe, ordering all things by number, weight, and measure." (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"Who has directed the Spirit of the LORD?"** (v.13) — Ellicott sees the Spirit here "clothed as with a Divine personality," answering to Wisdom in Proverbs 8:22–30. Eastern cosmogonies might depict gods consulting other deities; Isaiah knows no counsellor but One who is essentially one with the Eternal. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"The nations are like a drop in a bucket"** (v.15) — Ellicott: "Such a drop adds nothing to the weight which the bearer feels." The "isles" (or coastlands) are a favourite word of Isaiah, reflecting one who looks on the Mediterranean and thinks of unexplored regions. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"Lebanon is not sufficient for fuel"** (v.16) — Even the famously forested Lebanon, with all its beasts, could not provide an adequate sacrifice to the greatness of God (cf. Psalm 50:10–12). (Ellicott, Bible.org) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm ; https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-40

- **"Less than nothing and meaningless"** (v.17) — "Meaningless" is the Hebrew *tohu*, the same word for the formless void of Genesis 1:2. Human rulers and nations are *tohu* before YHWH. (Bible.org) https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-40

- **Guzik** emphasizes the anthropomorphic language: God is Spirit (John 4:24), but the vivid imagery communicates His incomparable greatness in terms we can grasp. (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-40/

---

### vv. 18–20: The Folly of Idolatry

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"To whom will you liken God?"** — Ellicott says the thought of God's infinity leads directly to the argument against idolatry, just as in Paul's reasoning at Athens (Acts 17:24–29). Isaiah's tone is sarcastic; Paul's is more pitying, reflecting their different audiences. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **The idol factory** (vv.19–20) — Ellicott notes the reign of Ahaz (and later Manasseh) supplied Isaiah with this picture as fully as if he had lived in Babylon. The rich have idols cast in metal, overlaid with gold, fitted with silver chains. The poor choose incorruptible wood and hire a skilled craftsman to make an idol that "will not topple." (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **Gill** notes v.20 describes one "so impoverished that he hath no oblation" — even the poor man scrapes together resources for an idol. The absurdity is that the same wood that could rot is selected, and the idol's chief virtue is simply that it stands upright. (Gill) https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/40.htm

---

### vv. 21–26: God Enthroned Above the Earth

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"Do you not know? Have you not heard?"** (v.21) — Ellicott says the verbs are potential futures: "Can you not know…?" Isaiah appeals to primary intuitions or primitive revelation, not merely the Decalogue (cf. Romans 1:20). (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"He sits enthroned above the circle of the earth"** (v.22) — "Circle" (*chug*) refers to the vault of heaven overarching the earth (Job 22:14; Proverbs 8:27). Earth's inhabitants are "like grasshoppers" — an image perhaps suggested by Numbers 13:33. God "stretches out the heavens like a curtain" — a favourite phrase of Isaiah 40–66 (42:5; 44:24), taken from Psalm 104:2. Ellicott notes this indicates "a clearer perception of space" than the older "firmament" of Genesis 1:7. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"He brings princes to nothing"** (v.23–24) — Rulers are hardly planted, hardly sown, before His breath withers them. Ellicott: "Such are empires before the eternity of Jehovah: so soon withered that we cannot say that they were ever really planted." (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"To whom will you liken Me?"** (v.25) — The Holy One's rhetorical question is the great monotheistic affirmation (cf. Deut 6:4–5; Exodus 8:10; 15:11; Micah 7:18). (Bible.org) https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-40

- **"He calls each one by name"** (v.26) — God marshals the starry host like a general who knows every soldier by sight and name, or a shepherd who knows his flock (John 10:3). "Not one of them is missing." (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

---

### vv. 27–31: Strength for the Weary

**Traditional Reading:**

- **"My way is hidden from the LORD"** (v.27) — Israel's complaint: God doesn't see my path or care about my cause. Guzik calls this "practical atheism" — knowing God exists but living as if He doesn't care about our personal struggles. (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-40/

- **"Do you not know? Have you not heard?"** (v.28) — The same questions of v.21, now addressed to Israel specifically. "The everlasting God … will not grow tired or weary." Ellicott asks whether Isaiah had learnt that his own earlier phrase about men "wearying God" (Isaiah 7:13) was too boldly anthropomorphic. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"His understanding is beyond searching out"** — Ellicott says these words "must have been in St. Paul's mind as he wrote Romans 11:33." (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"He gives power to the faint"** (v.29) — To them pre-eminently; their very consciousness of weakness is the condition of receiving strength (cf. Matthew 5:6; Luke 1:52–53). (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"Even youths grow tired and weary"** (v.30) — The second word (*bachurim*) implies young men at the peak of their vigour. Even these stumble. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **"Those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength"** (v.31) — "Wait" (*qavah*) implies expectant, active faith, not passive resignation. Ellicott: "For the faithful there is no failure, and faith knows no weariness." "Mount up with wings like eagles" — Ellicott says "shall put forth wings' feathers," reflecting the ancient belief that the eagle renewed its plumage in old age (cf. Psalm 103:5). (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

- **Precept Austin** expands: "waiting faith" is "faith that relies on and recalls the record of what God has done … rather than relying on an arm of flesh." It is a faith that "allows one to sit still and know that Jehovah is God (Ps 46:10)." The threefold progression (mount up, run, walk) covers all of life — the extraordinary moments, the intense seasons, and the day-by-day plodding. (Precept Austin) https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_4031_commentary

- **Guzik** stresses that waiting on the LORD is not passive but actively seeking and relying on Him. The progression from soaring to running to walking is not a decline but a picture of sustained endurance across all of life's circumstances. (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-40/

### Tradition-Specific Differences (Summary)

1. **Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill):** Tend toward a strongly Christological reading throughout. Gill sees vv.1–2 as referring to Gospel ministers and the "warfare" of the law ended by Christ. Spurgeon's emphasis on vv.6–8 is the Spirit's withering of human pride to make way for grace — a distinctly evangelical conversionist reading. (Spurgeon) https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-withering-work-of-the-spirit ; (Gill) https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/40.htm

2. **Reformed (Piper):** Emphasises God's glory as the ultimate end. Piper reads v.5 as pointing to the second coming, when Christ's glory will be revealed to all humanity — for some as Judge, for others as Saviour. God created the world for His glory; Isaiah 40 serves that theme. (Desiring God) https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/three-meditations-on-the-messiah ; https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/why-did-god-create-the-world/excerpts/live-to-make-god-look-good

3. **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik/Enduring Word):** Stresses personal application, heart preparation, and the active role of the believer in "waiting" on God. Guzik reads the chapter as addressing "practical atheism" in believers' lives and offers a warmly devotional tone throughout. (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-40/

4. **Anglican (Ellicott):** More restrained, historically grounded, attentive to Hebrew grammar and parallelism. Ellicott engages critical questions (e.g., authorship, the meaning of "double") without dogmatic heat. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/40.htm

5. **Evangelical (Bible.org / Bob Utley):** Emphasises the unity of Isaiah (rejecting multiple-authorship theories), reads chapters 40–66 through a pre-millennial, literal lens, notes the "new Exodus" motif and "new covenant" connections (Jeremiah 31:31–34). (Bible.org) https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-40
